### load the data

```{r}
install.packages("GWmodel")

# Load packages
library(sf)
library(spdep)
library(spatialreg)
library(GWmodel)
library(tidyverse)
library(tmap)
library(broom)
```

### load the shapefile

```{r}
philly <- st_read(
  "RegressionDataFiles.shp"
)
```

logaraithmic variables were already created in assignment 1, move onto
next step

### Queen-contiguity spatial weights

```{r}
# Check the coordinate system
st_crs(philly)

# Repair invalid geometries if necessary
philly <- st_make_valid(philly)

# Create Queen-contiguity neighbors
queen_nb <- poly2nb(
  philly,
  queen = TRUE
)

# Create row-standardized spatial weights
queen_weights <- nb2listw(
  queen_nb,
  style = "W",
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

# Check the neighbor structure
summary(queen_nb)
summary(card(queen_nb))
```

### Global Moran's I for median house values

```{r}
# Global Moran's I
moran.test(
  philly$LNMEDHVAL,
  queen_weights,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

# Randomization test with 999 permutations
set.seed(5080)

global_moran <- moran.mc(
  philly$LNMEDHVAL,
  queen_weights,
  nsim = 999,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)
```

```{r}
global_moran_res <- global_moran$res
hist(global_moran_res, freq = 10000000, nclass=100)
abline(v=moran(philly$LNMEDHVAL, queen_weights, n = length(queen_weights$neighbours), S0=Szero(queen_weights))$`I`, col='red')

```

### LISA: Local Moran's I

```{r}

lisa <- localmoran(
  philly$LNMEDHVAL,
  queen_weights,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

philly$local_I <- lisa[, "Ii"]
philly$local_p <- lisa[, "Pr(z != E(Ii))"]

# Map local Moran's I p-values
tm_shape(philly) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "local_p",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      breaks = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 1),
      values = c("darkblue", "blue", "lightblue", "pink"),
      labels = c("p < 0.001", "p < 0.01", "p < 0.05", "Not significant")
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "p-value")
  ) +
  tm_title("LISA P-Value Map: Median House Values")
```

```{r}
lisa <- localmoran(
  philly$LNMEDHVAL,
  queen_weights,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

# Attach local Moran statistics to the polygons
philly$local_I <- lisa[, "Ii"]
philly$local_p <- lisa[, "Pr(z != E(Ii))"]

# Standardize the variable and compute its spatial lag (neighbors' average)
philly$z_val <- as.numeric(scale(philly$LNMEDHVAL))
philly$lag_z <- lag.listw(queen_weights, philly$z_val, zero.policy = TRUE)

# Classify into quadrants, only where p < 0.05
sig <- 0.05
philly$cluster <- "Not significant"
philly$cluster[philly$z_val > 0 & philly$lag_z > 0 & philly$local_p < sig] <- "High-High"
philly$cluster[philly$z_val < 0 & philly$lag_z < 0 & philly$local_p < sig] <- "Low-Low"
philly$cluster[philly$z_val > 0 & philly$lag_z < 0 & philly$local_p < sig] <- "High-Low"
philly$cluster[philly$z_val < 0 & philly$lag_z > 0 & philly$local_p < sig] <- "Low-High"

philly$cluster <- factor(
  philly$cluster,
  levels = c("High-High", "Low-Low", "High-Low", "Low-High", "Not significant")
)

# Map the clusters
tm_shape(philly) +
  tm_polygons(
    "cluster",
    palette = c("#d7191c", "#2c7bb6", "#fdae61", "#abd9e9", "grey90"),
    title = "LISA Cluster",
    drop.levels = FALSE   # keep all categories in the legend
  ) +
  tm_layout(
    title = "LISA Clusters of Median House Values"
  )
```

### OLS Regression

```{r}
# Model formula
model_formula <- LNMEDHVAL ~
  PCTBACHMOR +
  PCTVACANT +
  PCTSINGLES +
  LNNBELPOV +
  MEDHHINC

# Fit OLS
ols_model <- lm(
  model_formula,
  data = philly
)

# Regression output
summary(ols_model)
```

### save the fitted values and residuals

```{r}
philly$OLS_PRED <- fitted(ols_model)
philly$OLS_RESID <- residuals(ols_model)
```

### test OLS residuals for spatial autocorrelation

```{r}
# Moran's I test for OLS residuals
moran.test(
  philly$OLS_RESID,
  queen_weights,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

set.seed(5080)

moran.mc(
  philly$OLS_RESID,
  queen_weights,
  nsim = 999,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)
```

### weighted residuals and scatterplot

```{r}
philly$WT_RESID <- lag.listw(
  queen_weights,
  philly$OLS_RESID,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

# Regress residuals on neighboring residuals
resid_model <- lm(
  OLS_RESID ~ WT_RESID,
  data = philly
)

summary(resid_model)

# Scatterplot with fitted regression line
ggplot(
  st_drop_geometry(philly),
  aes(x = WT_RESID, y = OLS_RESID)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "OLS Residuals vs. Spatially Lagged Residuals",
    x = "Weighted Average of Neighboring OLS Residuals",
    y = "OLS Residuals"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### spatial lag model

```{r}
lag_model <- lagsarlm(
  model_formula,
  data = philly,
  listw = queen_weights,
  zero.policy = TRUE,
  method = "eigen"
)

summary(lag_model)
```

### save residuals and test for spatial autocorrelation

```{r}
philly$LAG_RESID <- residuals(lag_model)

moran.test(
  philly$LAG_RESID,
  queen_weights,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

set.seed(5080)

moran.mc(
  philly$LAG_RESID,
  queen_weights,
  nsim = 999,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)
```

### run spatial error model

```{r}
error_model <- errorsarlm(
  model_formula,
  data = philly,
  listw = queen_weights,
  zero.policy = TRUE,
  method = "eigen"
)

summary(error_model)
```

### test the residuals

```{r}
philly$ERROR_RESID <- residuals(error_model)

moran.test(
  philly$ERROR_RESID,
  queen_weights,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

set.seed(5080)

moran.mc(
  philly$ERROR_RESID,
  queen_weights,
  nsim = 999,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)
```

### compare the three regression models

```{r}
model_comparison <- tibble(
  Model = c("OLS", "Spatial Lag", "Spatial Error"),
  AIC = c(
    AIC(ols_model),
    AIC(lag_model),
    AIC(error_model)
  ),
  R_squared = c(
    summary(ols_model)$r.squared,
    NA_real_,
    NA_real_
  )
)

model_comparison
```

### run geographically weighted regression (GWR)

#### prepare data

```{r}
# Project the data
philly_gwr <- st_set_crs(philly, 2272)

# Convert to Spatial format for GWmodel compatibility
philly_sp <- as(philly_gwr, "Spatial")

# Check coordinate system
st_crs(philly_gwr)
```

#### select bandwidth

```{r}
# Select bandwidth using AICc
gwr_bandwidth <- bw.gwr(
  model_formula,
  data = philly_sp,
  approach = "AICc",
  kernel = "bisquare",
  adaptive = TRUE
)

gwr_bandwidth
```

#### fit GWR

```{r}
gwr_model <- gwr.basic(
  model_formula,
  data = philly_sp,
  bw = gwr_bandwidth,
  kernel = "bisquare",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  F123.test = TRUE,
  cv = TRUE
)

# Global GWR diagnostics
gwr_model$GW.diagnostic
```

#### map local r-squared

```{r}
gwr_results <- st_as_sf(gwr_model$SDF)

names(gwr_results)
```

```{r}
ggplot(gwr_results) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = Local_R2), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Local R-squared",
    na.value = "grey80"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Local R-squared from Geographically Weighted Regression"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### test GWR residuals for spatial autocorrelation

```{r}
names(gwr_results)

# Save GWR residuals
philly$GWR_RESID <- gwr_results$residual

# Global Moran's I
moran.test(
  philly$GWR_RESID,
  queen_weights,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

# Permutation test
set.seed(5080)

gwr_moran <- moran.mc(
  philly$GWR_RESID,
  queen_weights,
  nsim = 999,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

gwr_moran
```

### map local coefficient to standard error ratios

```{r}
names(gwr_results)

# Example for one predictor
gwr_results <- gwr_results %>%
  mutate(
    ratio_PCTBACHMOR =
      PCTBACHMOR / PCTBACHMOR_SE
  )

gwr_results <- gwr_results %>%
  mutate(
    ratio_category = case_when(
      ratio_PCTBACHMOR < -2 ~ "Below -2",
      ratio_PCTBACHMOR < 0  ~ "-2 to 0",
      ratio_PCTBACHMOR <= 2 ~ "0 to 2",
      ratio_PCTBACHMOR > 2  ~ "Above 2",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    ratio_category = factor(
      ratio_category,
      levels = c(
        "Below -2",
        "-2 to 0",
        "0 to 2",
        "Above 2"
      )
    )
  )

ggplot(gwr_results) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = ratio_category), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Below -2" = "darkred",
      "-2 to 0" = "pink",
      "0 to 2" = "lightblue",
      "Above 2" = "darkblue"
    ),
    na.value = "grey80",
    name = "Coefficient / SE"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Local Coefficient-to-SE Ratio: Bachelor's Degree"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Introduction**


**Methods start**

The 1st Law of Geography states that near things are more related than
distant things. Moran’s I measures the degree of spatial autocorrelation
in our data, telling us whether data points with similar values are near
each other. The Moran’s I formula produces one number that explains
whether our data is positively autocorrelated (positive values, data
with similar values are near to each other), negatively autocorrelated
(negative values, data with high values are near to values with low
values), or have no spatial autocorrelation (very close to 0 or, more
precisely -1/(n-1), the data is randomly scattered). The formula is as
follows:

$$I = \frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} w_{ij}} \cdot \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} w_{ij}(x_i - \bar{x})(x_j - \bar{x})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2}$$

The explanation of the terms is as follows:

- $n$: the number of spatial units (for this model it is block groups)
- $x_i$: the value of the variable at location $i$
- $x_j$: the value of the variable at location $j$
- $\bar{x}$: the mean of the variable across $n$ locations
- $w_{ij}$: the spatial weight between locations $i$ and $j$ taken from
  the weight matrix
- $\sum_{i}\sum_{j} w_{ij}$: the sum of all weights
- $(x_i - \bar{x}) (x_j - \bar{x})$: the output of deviations from the
  mean
- $\sum_{i}(x_i - \bar{x})^2$: the sum of squared deviations from the
  mean, which shows the total variation in the variable

Throughout our report, we used a Queen contiguity weight matrix, meaning
we defined neighbors as block groups that share any point along borders.
Statisticians often use multiple spatial weight matrices in analyses to
measure the efficacy of their model. Given the various methods for
defining neighbors in spatial statistics, this gives the statistician
more tools to verify whether their model produces consistent results
with different spatial weight matrices, or whether the result is a
product of the specific spatial weight matrix they chose.

We use Moran’s I as a statistical test to determine if there is spatial
autocorrelation and if so, whether the data is positively or negatively
spatially autocorrelated. Our Moran’s I value was .79, indicating
positive spatial autocorrelation. Typically, negative spatial
autocorrelation ranges from -1 to near 0, and positive spatial
autocorrelation ranges from near 0 to 1. This shows that our data is
spatially clustered; in other words, data points with high values are
close to other data points with high values, and data points with low
values are near other points with low values.

We then want to know whether this pattern is statistically significant
or if it could have occurred by chance. The null hypothesis is that
there is no spatial autocorrelation, meaning there is no spatial pattern
to our data. The alternative hypothesis is that there is positive
autocorrelation. It is worth noting that the alternative hypothesis is
the presence of positive autocorrelation (not negative) because,
consistent with the First Law of Geography, we expect positive spatial
autocorrelation in geographic data and have thus, decided to run a
one-sided test. To test our hypothesis, we use a permutation test, which
takes all observed values, shuffles them, randomly reassigns them to the
map, and then recalculates Moran’s I. We repeat this 999 times. If fewer
than 5% of the 999 random permuted values are as large as or larger than
the originally observed Moran’s I value (when $/alpha$ = .05), we can
reject the null hypothesis. We calculated a pseudo p-value of .001,
meaning none of the 999 permuted values were as large or larger than the
original Moran’s I value. This indicates significance, and thus a we can
reject the null hypothesis.

The limitation of using the global Moran’s I is that it is a single
number that represents the entire data set, it does not indicate where
the spatial autocorrelation is. It tells us simply that spatial
clustering is happening. To identify more localized patterns of spatial
autocorrelation, we run Local Moran’s I, also known as the Local
Indicator of Spatial Association (LISA). Instead of measuring the
overall pattern of spatial autocorrelation like we do for the global
Moran’s I, the LISA goes block by block, calculating how similar that
block group is to the average of its neighbors.

Although the significance testing for the local Moran’s I works
differently from the permutation test we used for the global Moran’s I,
it answers the same question: is this observation unusual compared to
what a random distribution of data would produce? The following code
chunk calculates the local Moran’s I for each block group, compares each
value to its expected value under spatial randomness using a z-score,
and then derives a p-value from that z-score.

lisa \<- localmoran( philly\$LNMEDHVAL, queen_weights, zero.policy =
TRUE )

philly$local_I <- lisa[, "Ii"]
philly$local_p \<- lisa[, "Pr(z != E(Ii))"]

Because the null hypothesis assumes no spatial autocorrelation, the test
calculates what Local Moran’s I is expected to be if that were true. It
also calculates how much it would vary by chance alone. Then it compares
the observed Local Moran’s I value to the expected value using a
z-score. This measures how many standard deviations the observed value
is from the expected value if the null hypothesis were true.

We then mapped the LISA p-values. The map shows significant p-values in
dark blue (p \< .001), blue (p \< .01), and light blue (p \< .05), and
not significant values in pink (p ≥ .05). Pink means that we cannot tell
if that block group is part of a spatial pattern. There is not enough
evidence to say whether the block group is similar or different from its
neighbors, but the test indicates that it could conceivably happen by
chance alone.

As previously noted, neighbors in our model are defined by the Queen
matrix. Based on its relationship to the average of its neighbors, each
block group falls into one of four categories. We have found the
following schema helpful in conceptualizing these categories.

High-High: I am a high value block group and my neighbors are high value
block groups Low-Low: I am a low value block group and my neighbors are
low value block groups High-Low: I am a high value block group and my
neighbors are low value block groups Low-High: I am a low value block
group and my neighbors are high value block groups

We mapped these values, producing a result that appeared similar to the
LISA P-Value Map.

Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression is a type of linear regression
used to model the relationship between a dependent variable and one or
more independent variables. Statisticians use OLS for two primary
purposes: inference and prediction. Inferential analysis uses a sample
to draw conclusions about a population, and predictive analysis uses the
model to predict outcomes for unseen data. OLS chooses coefficients that
minimize the sum of squared residuals, defining the line or plane that
best fits the data. The OLS assumptions are as follows:

**Linearity.** The relationship between each predictor and the dependent
variable is assumed to be linear. If the true relationship curves, a
straight line will misstate the effect across parts of the range.

**Independence of observations.** Observations, and therefore their
residuals, are assumed to be independent of one another.

**Normality of residuals.** The errors are assumed to be normally
distributed with a mean of zero. Note that this applies to the residuals
rather than to the raw variables, which need not be normal themselves.

**Homoscedasticity.** The variance of the errors is assumed to be constant
across all levels of the predicted values. If instead the errors widen
or narrow systematically, a condition called heteroscedasticity, the
standard errors and the significance tests built on them may be
unreliable.

**Multicollinearity.** Predictors can be correlated with each other, but not
so strongly (e.g., \|r\| \> 0.8, or VIF above 4, and especially above
10) that the model can’t separate their effects. Severe
multicollinearity makes coefficients unstable and inflates their
standard errors.

**Observations.** No fewer than 10 observations per predictor.

Our previous report goes further into depth about OLS, which you can
read here.

When the data has a spatial component, the OLS assumption that errors are
independent is often violated. We can test this by calculating the
Moran’s I of the residuals, which analyzes spatial autocorrelation of
the residuals. Another way to test OLS residuals for spatial
autocorrelation is to regress them on nearby residuals. If the
independence assumption holds, block group’s residuals shouldn’t have
much to do with their neighbors. We visualized this by creating a
scatterplot of the OLS residuals and the weighted average of neighboring
OLS residuals. The slope of the regression line was .731, for every one
unit increase in the average residual of a block group’s neighbor, that
block group’s own residual is expected to increase by about .73. Simply
put, block groups whose neighbors were under or over predicted, tend to
be under or over predicted in the same direction. The first step in
calculating the slope is finding the average of the OLS residuals of
neighboring block groups. Then the OLS residuals are regressed on the
average of the neighbor’s OLS residuals. The slope measures the extent
to which the two variables move together, divided by the variance of the
neighbors’ average residuals. Plainly, it is the expected change of the
block group’s residuals for each one-unit increase in the average
residual of its neighbor.

R, the tool we used to run the regression, can also test other
regression assumptions, such as homoscedasticity, which is also related
to the assumption of independence of errors. R has specific packages
designed to run the Breusch-Pagan, Koenker-Bassett, and White test,
which determine whether the variance of the residuals changes with the
predictors. In these tests, the null hypothesis is that the errors are
homoscedastic and the alternative hypothesis is that the errors are
heteroscedastic. A p-value < .05 means we reject the null hypothesis,
while a p-value > .05 means we fail to reject the null hypothesis,
indicating there is no significant evidence of heteroscedasticity.

R can also test the assumption of normality of errors with a package
that runs the Jarque-Bera test. The null hypothesis is that the errors
are normally distributed and the alternative hypothesis is that the
errors are not normally distributed. A p-value < .05 means we reject
the null hypothesis and conclude that the residuals are not normal,
while a p-value > .05 means we fail to reject the null hypothesis and
conclude that the residuals are normal.

We used R to run spatial lag and spatial error regressions. Unlike OLS,
the spatial lag model assumes spatial dependence. The model accounts for
this dependence by adding an extra predictor to the OLS model: the
average dependent variable of each neighbor, or in our case, the average
house value of each block group’s neighbors (W * LNMEDHVAL).

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{LNMEDHVAL} = \; & \rho W \cdot \text{LNMEDHVAL} + \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{PCTBACHMOR} + \beta_2 \text{PCTVACANT} \\
& + \beta_3 \text{PCTSINGLES} + \beta_4 \text{LNNBELPOV} + \beta_5 \text{MEDHHINC} + \varepsilon
\end{aligned}$$

**W** is our queen weights and **LNMEDHVAL** is our dependent
variable, log median house values for all block groups 

Which means,

$W * LNMEDHVAL$ is the spatially lagged dependent variable: the average log
median house value of each block group’s neighbors. 

$\rho$ measures the strength of spatial dependence: how much a block group’s house value
depends on its neighbors’ house values.

$\beta_0$ is the intercept, $\beta_1$ through $\beta_5$ are the coefficients for each predictor
in the error term

We also used a spatial error model in our analysis, which accounts for
spatial dependencies in the unobserved factors that could impact our
dependent variable. In contrast to the spatial lag model that says house
value is influenced directly by surrounding house values, the spatial
error model says that house values in a similar region are subject to
the same unobserved conditions.

$$ \begin{aligned} \text{LNMEDHVAL} = \; & \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{PCTBACHMOR} + \beta_2 \text{PCTVACANT} \\& + \beta_3 \text{PCTSINGLES} + \beta_4 \text{LNNBELPOV} + \beta_5 \text{MEDHHINC} + \varepsilon \end{aligned} $$

$$ \varepsilon = \lambda W \varepsilon + u $$

* $\beta_0$ is the intercept, and $\beta_1$ through $\beta_5$ are the coefficients for each
  predictor.
* $\varepsilon$ is the error term from the main regression, the part of house values
  the predictors don’t explain.
* $W$ is the spatially lagged error: the average error of each block
  group’s neighbors, as defined by the Queen matrix.
* $\lambda$ measures how strongly a block group’s error is related to its
  neighbors’ errors.
* $u$ is the remaining random error, which should be independent and free
  of spatial autocorrelation. 
  
The other OLS assumptions also pertain to Spatial Lag and Spatial Error models, 
with the exception of spatial independence of observations. The goal of these 
models is to account for spatial dependence, resulting in a better fitting 
model withhigher rates of reliability. We are able to measure the accuracy of 
our model with various metrics. First, we can look at the Moran’s I of 
residuals. The value should be closer to 0 than the OLS Moran’s I of residuals 
and ideally not statistically significant. If the spatial models work, the 
spatial lag term (ρ) or spatial error term (λ) will capture the spatial 
patterns, instead of leaving them in the residuals. We also compare each model 
by using the Akaike Information Criterion/Schwarz Criterion, Log Likelihood, 
and the Likelihood Ratio Test. These criteria are only valid when the models 
being compared share the same dependent variable and are fit to the same set of
observations, which is the case for all three models in this analysis.Each 
criterion also has its own characteristics and requirements, which are 
discussed below. The Akaike Information Criterion/Schwarz Criterion are measures 
of goodness of fit. We use them when we want to compare models while accounting 
for complexity because it penalizes each additional parameter. When comparing 
AIC across models, we opt for a lower value because it indicates the model fits 
well without unnecessary parameters. AIC is only useful for comparing models. We
can use the AIC to compare nested and non-nested models.

We use Log Likelihood as a measure of fit, by scoring how well the model matches 
the observed data. A higher score indicates that the observed data is more 
probably under the model, meaning a better fit. We get the score by multiplying 
the likelihood value of each block group In our data, this would require 
multiplying 1,720 block group values, resulting in a number so extreme, it 
could easily become unmanageable. Instead, the Log Likelihood, takes the log of 
each value, which by the rules of logarithms, turns the multiplication into
addition. Because Log Likelihood doesn’t penalize additional parameters, it is 
important to use it alongside AIC. 

Log Likelihood can be used when comparing nested and non-nested models. The 
Likelihood Ratio Test measures if a more complex model fits the data 
significantly better than a simpler one. It uses log likelihood to measure the 
fit of two models, one more complex than the other, for example a model that 
accounts for spatial dependency and an OLS model. It then compares the two log 
likelihood scores and runs a test to check whether the difference is big enough 
to reliably not be attributable to random chance. The Likelihood Ratio statistic 
follows a chi-squared distribution where the degrees of freedom are equal to
the difference in the number of parameters between the two models. For our 
model, the df = 1 because each spatial model adds one parameter. The Likelihood 
Ratio Test can only be used on nested models. Because of this, we cannot compare 
spatial lag and spatial error models. In this case, they can only be compared to 
OLS. The null hypothesis in the Likelihood Ratio Test is always that the complex 
model is not a better fit than the simpler model. Using the spatial lag and 
spatial error models as examples, the null and alternative hypotheses are as
follows: 

For the spatial lag model:
  
* $H₀: ρ = 0$ The spatial lag model is not a better fit than OLS.
* $H₁: ρ ≠ 0$ The spatial lag model is a better fit than OLS. 

For the spatial error model:

* $H₀: λ = 0$ The spatial error model is not a better fit than OLS.
* $H₁: λ ≠ 0$ The spatial error model is a better fit than OLS. If the
  p-value is less than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude
  that the spatial model fits significantly better than OLS.

We ran our Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) analyses in R. GWR
runs a separate local regression for each block group, using a
proximity-based weighting scheme that gives closer neighbors more
influence on the local regression coefficient than farther neighbors.
Simpson’s paradox describes the seemingly enigmatic condition in which a
global pattern in the dataset disappears or reverses when the data is
divided into subgroups. A single global regression may misrepresent
local relationships that cannot be captured with a single statistic.
This paradox is common in spatial data because relationships between the
dependent variable and predictors vary across space, a state called
spatial non-stationarity. GWR uniquely addresses this. In the case of
our model, the relationship between vacancy and house values may differ
substantially between neighborhoods in Philadelphia, but we wouldn’t be
able to tell based on a single global statistic. 

GWR uses what is called a bandwidth to determine which neighboring observations 
are included in the local analysis. There are two types of bandwidths: fixed and
adaptive. Fixed bandwidth uses a fixed distance from the regression
point outward in all directions, this means the area also remains
constant for each local regression. In other words, a fixed bandwidth
uses the same sized net to capture its neighboring observations and it
is most effective when observations are relatively uniformly distributed
across space. Conversely, adaptive bandwidth is best used when
observations vary widely across space, when events are concentrated in
one area and sparse in others. Unlike the fixed bandwidth’s same sized
net analogy, adaptive bandwidth’s range is dictated by the number of
neighboring observations it captures. The net’s size may change, but the
number of neighboring observations remains the same. We use adaptive
bandwidth in our model because the observations in our data are not
uniformly distributed across space, they vary quite a bit given where in
the city the block group is. Block groups are small and dense in Center
City and larger in the Northeast and Northwest areas of Philadelphia. If
we were to use fixed bandwidth for this data, we would capture many
block groups downtown and very few at the edges of th city. 

GWR runs by attributing a value to each coefficient at each location. This means
that our model ran a weighted regression for every 1,720 block groups.
It does this by selecting a block group, assigning weights to nearby
block groups based on the bandwidth, running a weighted regression using
those weights, saving those coefficients as those block groups local
coefficients, and then repeating that process for each block group. The
GWR equation for our model is as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{LNMEDHVAL}_i = \; & \beta_0(u_i, v_i) + \beta_1(u_i, v_i)\,\text{PCTBACHMOR}_i + \beta_2(u_i, v_i)\,\text{PCTVACANT}_i \\
& + \beta_3(u_i, v_i)\,\text{PCTSINGLES}_i + \beta_4(u_i, v_i)\,\text{LNNBELPOV}_i + \beta_5(u_i, v_i)\,\text{MEDHHINC}_i + \varepsilon_i
\end{aligned}$$

* $i$ refers to an individual block group
* $(ui,vi)$ are the coordinates of block group i
* $\beta_0(ui,vi)$ is the local intercept at block group i
- $\beta_1(ui,vi)$ through $\beta_5(ui,vi)$ are the local coefficients for each
  predictor at block group i, which can vary across space
- $\varepsilon_i$ is the error term for block group i.

The local coefficients are estimated using weighted least squares:
$$ \hat{\beta}(u_i, v_i) = (X^T W_i X)^{-1} X^T W_i y $$ 


The OLS assumptions are the same for GWR. One assumption even becomes
more stringent: no severe multicollinearity. This is because GWR makes
multicollinearity more likely and potentially more potent. Each local
regression relies primarily on neighboring observations, which means
limited variation and less total amount of data per regression point.
Also, because nearby block groups tend to have similar characteristics,
predictors that are only moderately correlated across the city can be
highly correlated within a local neighborhood. When predictors are
highly correlated, the regression cannot identify which variable
produces which outcome, resulting in unstable coefficients and
potentially creating spatial patterns that may look deceptively
meaningful. We can check for multicollinearity using the condition
number. The condition number measures the degree of multicollinearity in
a set of predictors. It is calculated for each local regression and if
it reads greater than 30, we generally cannot trust its results. While
stationarity isn’t named as a formal assumption of OLS, it is implicit
in the mechanics of the equation. GWR, also implies stationarity,
although it takes on a different meaning. OLS assumes global
stationarity; GWR assumes local stationarity.

**Methods end**
